extracted.intended_audience: plant physiologists, botanists and experimental biologists researching long-distance transport in plants
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and experimental approaches for determining whether organic substances and signals are transported longitudinally in plants via the bast (phloem/sieve-tubes) or the tracheae of the wood (xylem), including quantitative estimates, tracer experiments, tissue-killing tests, and physiological manipulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determination of transport channel (bast vs wood)
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide whether organic substances are distributed through the plant 'by means of the bast' (sieve-tubes) or 'in the tracheæ of the wood' (xylem).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weigh experimental results such as ringing, petiole sectioning, and anaesthetisation of petioles (Czapek) against criticisms and counter-experiments (Deleano, Strasburger). Consider whether killing or damaging outer tissues truly leaves the wood uninjured (microscopic examination may show tracheae blocked after bark removal). A transport channel hypothesis must be consistent with anatomical observations and with experiments in which transport continues or ceases after removal/killing of living tissues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical plausibility via quantitative estimates (volumes, cross-sections, velocities)
rubrics_metrics.description: Estimate the quantities of organic material transported and the velocities required given the cross-sectional area of proposed conduits; use these to test feasibility of a candidate channel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two methods recommended: (1) infer from amount accumulated in a storage organ (example: potato tuber mass, bast cross-section, assumed sugar concentration) and (2) infer from amount exported from an assimilating organ (photosynthesis rate per leaf area, petiole bast cross-section). Use realistic concentrations (bleeding sap values often <4%) and include possible non-functional area (cell-walls). Example calculations in the text yield required velocities in the order of 20–140 cm per hour for bast conduits, which are argued to be implausibly high for sieve-tubes. Compare computed velocities with known physical constraints of the tissue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tracer/dye experiments to map direction and continuity of flow
rubrics_metrics.description: Use soluble tracers (eosin, lithium nitrate, etc.) to follow the paths of fluid movement into and through tracheae/vascular bundles and to demonstrate upward and downward currents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: cutting a leaf tip under eosin solution rapidly colours tracheae of leaf and petiole and can inject tuber tracheae; splitting a petiole and placing half in eosin shows unilateral uptake and subsequent spread according to anatomical connections. Tracer patterns reveal that some tracheal filaments receive the coloured stream while neighbouring filaments remain uncoloured, showing isolated linear series and path-of-least-resistance behaviour. Use tracers to demonstrate reversed currents and to map which conducting tracheae communicate with subterranean organs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tissue-killing / disruption tests
rubrics_metrics.description: Test whether transport persists when living tissues are killed or removed (e.g., by heat, chloroform vapour, jacketing, or physical removal of bark/outer tissues).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Czapek's petiole-killing results suggested reliance on living protoplasm; Deleano and others showed continued depletion after killing, implying dead conduits can transmit. Ricca's experiments removing large lengths of bast and showing stimulus transmission suggest wood involvement. Such tests help discriminate a living-cell-mediated mechanism from transport in dead conduits, but must account for secondary effects (e.g., clogging, air embolism, exudation) and be corroborated by microscopic and tracer evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Microscopic examination of conduits after manipulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Perform microscopic inspection of wood and associated tissues after manipulations such as ringing to assess blocking, air-embolism, exudation into tracheae, and discoloration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author notes that wood from which outer tissues have been stripped shows tracheae soon become blocked with air-bubbles and exuded substances, especially in outer wood layers, and discoloration accompanies blocking. Such anatomical/ultrastructural findings explain why ringing can impair transport and must be considered when interpreting functional experiments that depend on removing bark or cambium.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for sieve-tube and pit anatomy and colloid content
rubrics_metrics.description: Any model proposing mass transport through the bast/sieve-tubes must address the narrow transverse sections, frequent transverse walls, sieve-plate pores, and colloidal/protoplasmic contents that impede bulk flow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author argues that the narrowness, transverse walls and colloid-filled sieve-pores make the high velocities required implausible. Simple diffusion cannot account for observed rates; adsorption on colloidal surfaces is unlikely to increase effective transport sufficiently. Be explicit about sieve-pore dimensions and colloid effects when evaluating phloem-based bulk flow hypotheses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonstration of hormone-mediated stimulus transmission via vascular bundles
rubrics_metrics.description: Show that stimuli (phototropic, geotropic, traumatic, etc.) are transmitted by dissolved substances (hormones) conveyed in vascular channels, often across killed or protoplasm-discontinuous tissue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use experiments like Ricca (Mimosa) where stimulus transmission persists through dead/water-filled channels, Boysen-Jensen and Padl (transmission across protoplasmic discontinuities or gelatine disks), and Stark (thermostability and partial specificity) to argue for dissolved-hormone transport. Measure transmission speeds and compare to diffusion to support convective vascular transport. Specificity tests (grafting perceptive tips between plants) can indicate biochemical identity/compatibility of hormones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence for reversed transpiration currents in wood
rubrics_metrics.description: Demonstrate that wood tracheae can carry downstream (basipetal) as well as upward (acropetal) currents under physiological conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tracer experiments (eosin, lithium nitrate) and anatomical observations show selective downward movement in some tracheal filaments while others carry upward sap; Ricca's and Birchs-Hirschfeld's work are cited. Consider transpiration-driven local sinks/sources, anatomical isolation of linear tracheal series, and Strasburger's findings on high transverse resistance when interpreting the directionality of flow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manipulation of leaf turgor and permeability to test release into tracheae
rubrics_metrics.description: Use volume-change measurements, pressure chambers and permeability-modifying treatments (toluene, gas-pressure) to test whether cell-contents (carbohydrates) can be displaced into tracheae and contribute to downward flow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure leaf volume contractions and compute potential downward displacements (text gives examples producing velocities ~120 cm/hr). Pressure-chamber experiments forcing water from leaves were reported to yield practically pure water unless permeability was increased (e.g., with toluene), after which carbohydrate-containing fluid emerged and reduced Benedict’s solution. Surrounding a pinna with toluene vapour and tracing browning in wood can indicate cell-content movement into tracheae.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compare observed transport rates to diffusion limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Contrast measured velocities of stimulus or carbohydrate movement with expected diffusion speeds in tissue to decide whether convective vascular transport is necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author lists representative transmission velocities (e.g., Mimosa 0.07 mm/s, seedling light/gravity 180–300 mm/min?) and gives diffusion in tissue rates (2250–3600 [units in text]); use these comparisons to rule out simple diffusion when observed transport is much faster and to justify vascular/hormone-mediated mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional role hypothesis for the bast as exchange surface
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate the bast not primarily as a bulk longitudinal conduit, but as a living-surface system providing maximum interchange between living cells and dead conduits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider that the bast's small longitudinal cross-section but large surface facing the tracheae may be adapted for exchange (abstracting/introducing organic substances) rather than for providing the main translocation stream. Experiments and anatomical reasoning should test this interface/exchange role.
